lessons.title: Hear chha — six
lessons.gloss: six — four's opening consonant, with the breath added

segments.text: Recall the counting payoff, say tea, then say four.

segments.instruction: chār from the last chapter, and the plain ch you tested with a hand at your mouth
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: *chār* from the last chapter, and the plain *ch* you tested with a hand at your mouth]

segments.text: chha — six.
Hand at the mouth again. chār moves nothing. chha pushes a puff of air out with the consonant.

That single difference is the whole of it. The tongue does the same thing in both words; the lungs do not. Marwari keeps that contrast everywhere, and here it separates two numbers that sit next to each other on a price ticket.
The same number is also printed chhe, with a vowel mark after the consonant. Both are in use; count with the bare form for now and read the other when a page prints it.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

segments.prompt: Say four and six one after the other, and name what changes.
acceptedResponses: chār chha — the puff of air

feedback.incorrect: The tongue does not move between them; the air does.

lessons.title: छ (chha) — six on the page
lessons.gloss: six, on the page — one sign, and a second spelling that ends a word you know

segments.text: Write य, write ए, then write four.
छ — chha — six.
One sign, made in chapter 9, and nothing added to it.

The other printed spelling is छे, and it is worth a moment. That is छ (chha) with the mark of the letter chapter 32 taught — the same vowel, riding on a consonant instead of standing alone. It is also, exactly, the second syllable of पाछे. A chunk the hand has been writing since chapter 9 turns out to be a number.
Write छ (chha), then write छे beneath it, then write ए beside both. Say which of the three stands alone and which two need something under them.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Unicode Devanagari chart.

feedback.correct: The breathed छ, on its own.
feedback.incorrect: Six is the breathed छ, not the plain च.

lessons.title: Hear sāt — seven
lessons.gloss: seven — opening on the syllable this whole book opened on

segments.text: Give the greeting this book opened with, then say six and three.

segments.instruction: tīn and its long vowel, two chapters back
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: *tīn* and its long vowel, two chapters back]

segments.text: sāt — seven.
The first syllable is sā. That is the respect particle at the end of राम-राम सा, the first thing this book ever taught. The sound has been in the ear since page one; only its job here is new.
Seven closes on the dental t of tīn, not the retroflex one. Front of the mouth at both ends.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

segments.prompt: Count aloud from five to seven.

feedback.incorrect: Five, then the breathed one, then the one that opens like the greeting.

lessons.title: सात (sāt) — seven on the page
lessons.gloss: seven, on the page — three signs from the book's first four chapters

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Write tea, then write six.
सा + त becomes सात — sāt — seven.
सा was the second word-piece this book asked the hand to build, in chapter.
Seven is that piece with a dental त after it, and nothing else.
Look at सात (sāt), cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Then write तीन under it and mark the त in both.
Source: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani.

feedback.incorrect: Build it in two chunks: सा + त.

lessons.title: Hear āṭh — eight
lessons.gloss: eight — the one number that opens on a standing vowel the hand already had

segments.text: Recall the seven-word food payoff, offer formal thanks, then say seven.

segments.instruction: chār and pāṅch, and which of the two carries a nasal
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: *chār* and *pāṅch*, and which of the two carries a nasal]

segments.text: āṭh — eight.
It opens on the long ā of आभार, standing on its own with no consonant in front of it. Of the ten numbers this slice teaches, eight is the only one that does that.
The closing consonant is retroflex: the tongue curls back, as in ठंडी. Do not close it at the teeth, or seven and eight begin to sound alike.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

segments.prompt: Say seven and eight, and name where the tongue ends in each.
acceptedResponses: sāt at the teeth, āṭh curled back

feedback.correct: Front for seven, back for eight.
feedback.incorrect: Seven closes on the dental त; eight closes on the retroflex ठ.

lessons.title: आठ (āṭh) — eight on the page
lessons.gloss: eight, on the page — two signs, and neither of them new

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Write formal thanks, then write seven.
आ + ठ becomes आठ — āṭh — eight.
Two letters, both of them years old in this book's own timeline: आ from chapter 2 and ठ from chapter 17. Nothing is joined, nothing is marked.
Compare सात (sāt) and आठ (āṭh) side by side. Seven takes the vowel as a mark on a consonant; eight takes the same vowel as a letter, because there is no consonant for it to sit on.
Look at आठ (āṭh), cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Then write सात (sāt) above it and circle the long ā in each.
Source: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani.

feedback.correct: The standing आ, then the retroflex ठ.
feedback.incorrect: Eight begins with the letter आ, not with a consonant.

lessons.title: Hear no — nine
lessons.gloss: nine — two sounds, and it rhymes with the two you learned first

segments.text: Say this one, say very, then say eight.

segments.instruction: ek and the letter ए you had to learn to write it
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: *ek* and the letter **ए** you had to learn to write it]

segments.text: no — nine.
One consonant, one long vowel, and it rhymes with do. Two and nine are the only numbers in this run that short.

This is not the English word no. Marwadi has not yet given this book any word for refusing at all, which is a real gap and not a spelling accident: a learner who mishears no as a refusal will walk away from a fair price.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

segments.prompt: Which earlier number rhymes with nine?

feedback.correct: Both are one consonant plus long o.

lessons.title: नो (no) — nine on the page
lessons.gloss: nine, on the page — the same two-sign shape as two, with a different consonant

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Write this one, then write eight.
न + ो becomes नो — no — nine.
Write दो and नो (no) one under the other. The mark on the right is the same in both. Only the letter carrying it changes, and with it the number.
Look at नो (no), cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Then write दो beside it and read the pair aloud without looking.
Source: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani.

feedback.correct: One mark, two consonants, two numbers.
feedback.incorrect: Both take ो; nine takes न and two takes द.

lessons.title: Hear das — ten
lessons.gloss: ten — the first amount a market actually names

segments.text: Say show it to me, say five, then say nine.

segments.instruction: chha and the puff of air that separates it from chār
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: *chha* and the puff of air that separates it from *chār*]

segments.text: das — ten.
Short vowel this time, closed off at once by s. Nothing is held.

das is the first number in this book that a Rajasthani market is likely to say out loud. Almost nothing on a stall is priced under ten, which is why a course that stopped at five could ask the price four different ways and still not understand the answer.
The comparative dictionary of the Indo-Aryan languages lists this form for Marwari by name, under the Sanskrit word for ten.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

segments.prompt: Count aloud from six to ten.

feedback.incorrect: Six, seven, eight, nine, and the short one: das.

lessons.title: दस (das) — ten on the page
lessons.gloss: ten, on the page — built out of pieces of two other numbers

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Write ख, then write nine.
द + स becomes दस — das — ten.
Bare consonants. No mark rides above the line and none hangs below it, because the vowel between them is the short a that every Devanagari consonant carries without being told.
The द is two's; the स is seven's. Ten is written out of pieces the hand already made for other numbers.
Look at दस (das), cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Then write दो beside it and say what the mark on the second one does to the vowel.
Source: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani.

feedback.correct: Two bare consonants and the short a that comes free.

lessons.title: Ten words, shuffled
lessons.gloss: the second five, shuffled, and the first five brought back with them

segments.text: Write the show-request word, recall the counting payoff from the last chapter, then write ए.
Two runs of five are still two runs until they are mixed.
Hear ten numbers named singly, drawn from across the whole set, and say each.
Count backwards from ten to one.
Read आठ (āṭh), तीन, दस (das), छ (chha), एक, नो (no) printed in that order and say each.
Write सात (sāt), पांच, नो (no), दो, दस (das) from dictation.
Then say which pairs share a sign: two and nine, seven and ten, four and five.
Source: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani.

feedback.correct: Retrieved out of sequence, which is how a price arrives.
feedback.incorrect: Eight opens on a standing vowel; ten carries no mark at all.

lessons.title: Payoff — counting to ten
lessons.headword: एक दो तीन चार पांच छ सात आठ नो दस
lessons.romanization: ek do tīn chār pāṅch chha sāt āṭh no das
lessons.gloss: payoff — one to ten in listening, speaking, reading, and writing

segments.text: Recall the five-number payoff, then write the letter that made it possible.
Four skills, scored separately.
Listening. Hear ten numbers named singly and out of order; write each in figures of your own language.
Speaking. Count one to ten, then ten to one, with no model.
Reading. Read all ten printed in Devanagari, shuffled, and say each.
Writing. Write all ten from dictation, shuffled, with no model in view.
Pass each one separately.

Look back at what the hand had to learn for this: one letter, ए. Every other sign in all ten words was already in the book. A reader who felt the numbers were going to be a wall of new writing has the evidence in front of them that they were not.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9.

segments.prompt: Complete all four scored checks, then write one and ten side by side.

feedback.correct: One to ten now passes in all four skills.
feedback.incorrect: Repair only the failed skill, then retry that part.

lessons.title: Close the writing loop for छ (chha), ठ and स
lessons.gloss: delayed closure for the three consonants the second five lean on

segments.text: Recall the ten-number payoff, say the show request, then write market.
Write three single signs from sound cues: छ (chha), ठ, स. Then write च beside छ (chha) and mark which of the two carries the breath.
Then write छ (chha), सात (sāt), आठ (āṭh), नो (no), दस (das) from dictation. Repair only the missed sign and rewrite its word once.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Unicode Devanagari chart.

segments.prompt: Write the sign that opens six, then the sign that opens four.

feedback.incorrect: Six carries the breath: छ. Four does not: च.
